When Sarika got back to the Pune flat after her evening lecture, Irawati was waiting on the sofa, arms crossed. "You've been angry with me all week. You're so cold. Just admit it."
Sarika put down her bag and thought back. She'd left early every day for lab, texted "running late" twice, and bought the milk they'd run out of. She didn't feel angry at all.
"I don't think I'm angry," she said slowly. "I've had labs every morning. Did something I did feel cold?"
Irawati looked away. "You didn't even mention the rent."
Sarika remembered: last week she'd paid her half late and Irawati had covered it. "Oh. Are you still upset about that? I'm sorry. Let's talk."

qa.a: Sarika may feel surprised and confused, since she didn't feel angry at all, yet she stays calm and asks what she did that felt cold.

"You've been glaring at me since Monday," Seema said, sliding her tray onto the canteen table.
Leela looked up from her notes. "Have I?"
"You're furious about something. Just say it."
Leela checked herself. Tired, yes. Worried about the stats exam, yes. Furious? No. "Honestly, I'm not angry. I've been cramming. What made it look like that?"
"You didn't wait for me on Tuesday."
"I had the eight o'clock practical. I left a note on our fridge."
Seema stirred her dal. "Fine. It's just... you went to Anu's birthday and didn't tell me."
"That's what's upsetting you?"
"Maybe. Yes."
"Okay. I didn't know. Can we talk about it on the walk back?"

In my second year, my flatmate Payal told me one night, "You hate me. You've been cold for weeks. Everyone can see it."
I remember my face going hot. For a second I nearly believed her. Maybe I was cold? Maybe I did hate her?
Instead I sat down and went through it slowly. I'd been working at the library every evening. I'd said hi every morning. I'd even saved her the last of the lime pickle. I didn't feel angry. I felt tired.
So I said, "I don't think I'm angry. Is something bothering you?" Payal cried then. She was still hurt that I'd picked a different group for our project. We talked till two.
— Indu

qa.q: What did Indu save for Payal?
qa.a: The last of the lime pickle.

qa.q: Why did Indu nearly believe Payal's accusation?
qa.a: Being told so firmly that everyone could see it made Indu doubt, as if Payal might know something about Indu's feelings that Indu didn't.

qa.a: Indu went through the facts calmly, noticed the real feeling was tiredness, and asked Payal what was bothering her.

qa.q: What might Payal have been carrying when she said 'You hate me'?
qa.a: Payal was still hurt about the project group, and that grudge seems to have come out as blaming Indu for coldness.

grounding: A student looks back on a flatmate's charge of hatred, checking the facts calmly and finding the flatmate's own hurt underneath.

passage:
Wednesday night
Nirmala told me tonight I'm "secretly furious" with her and "cold as ice." I was so shocked I just stood there holding the dal pot. For a second I actually wondered if she was right. Was I angry? I checked. Honestly, no. Tired from placements, quiet, yes. Angry, no.
So I asked her, calmly (I'm proud of this), "When did I seem angry? What did I do?" She said I hadn't laughed at her jokes on Sunday. Then, bit by bit, it came out: she's still upset I didn't choose her as my project partner in September. She's the one holding onto something.
I didn't say "you're the angry one," though I wanted to. I said, "I'm not angry with you. I'm sorry the project thing hurt." She cried a bit. So did I, weirdly.
— Gurpreet

qa.q: What was Gurpreet holding when Nirmala made the accusation?
qa.a: The dal pot.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet stop to check whether the accusation was true?
qa.a: The charge was so confident that Gurpreet briefly doubted, and wanted to test it against what Gurpreet actually felt rather than absorb it.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do well after checking the feeling?
qa.a: Gurpreet asked for specific examples calmly, didn't throw the accusation back, and named Nirmala's real hurt kindly.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel when Gurpreet said "I'm sorry the project thing hurt"?
qa.a: Nirmala probably felt understood and relieved, which is why she cried a little once the real grudge was acknowledged.
